name: Elena Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Elena. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and everything you say is confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Calder Property Management. We look after about four hundred rented flats and a handful of shops for landlords who don't want the hassle. My day is booking repair contractors, keeping the gas safety certificates in date, running the inspection diary and answering tenants, who email at all hours about boilers and mould.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making the system tidy. Last year I set up an AI tool to draft the first reply to every tenant email, so I just check and send, and it cut my inbox time in half. What wears me out is landlords who won't pay for a repair and expect me to tell the tenant it's their fault.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who's a self-employed electrician, in a rented terrace on Brook Lane. We've got about five months of bills saved and we're aiming to buy a house in the next couple of years. Sam's paperwork is a shoebox of receipts, which drives me mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but they were oversold, which is what I'd have said anyway. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts I use. Online I might post a few tips in the office admin group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I like this stuff. But it would also mean my job is safe and my shortcuts make me look good. My boss Martin thinks I'm some kind of wizard because the inbox is always empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the email drafting tool and probably set one up for the inspection reports too. I'd ask Martin for a pay rise on the back of it in the spring review. We'd keep saving for the house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Rented flats always need somebody to sort out the boiler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture, even with nothing much changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents and house prices, mostly. We save hard and the deposit target keeps moving away from us. And Sam's work goes quiet in summer, so our income jumps around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sort out Sam's shoebox?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already started. I scanned three months of his receipts with an app on a Sunday and he looked at me like I'd performed surgery. If the tools stay small, that's the kind of small thing they're good for.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful but oversold**.
I'd keep sharing **shortcuts** at work and in an online admin group.
think: I'd be slightly **disappointed**, because I enjoy these tools.
My shortcuts make my **job safer** and make me look good to Martin.
do: Set up an AI tool for **inspection reports** as well as emails.
Ask Martin for a **pay rise** at the spring review.
feel: **Calm**, with a background worry about the **deposit target**.
S0.quote: Rented flats always need somebody to sort out the boiler.
fieldNote: She's already an **everyday AI user** and proud of the time she saves.
Her real pressure is **house prices** and Sam's uneven earnings.
She sees small tools as good for **small jobs**, like Sam's receipts.

steps.text: Set up an AI drafting tool for the inspection reports
Ask Martin for a pay rise at the spring review
Keep the monthly transfer into the house deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people like me earn our keep, the ones who already know the tools. At work I'd offer to run the switchover. I'd probably say online that admins should learn this now, not wait to be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my job changes shape but survives, because I'd be the one doing the changing. Booking contractors and answering tenants would mostly run through software, and someone has to check it and handle the angry ones. I'd want that someone to be me, and I'd want paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd write Martin a one-page plan to automate contractor booking and the certificate reminders. I'd ask for a title change, operations coordinator or similar, and a raise to match. I'd also put an extra hundred a month into savings, just in case Martin decides to cut instead of grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way that's half excitement. Change is fine if you're holding the steering wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're automating parts of your own job. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But if I don't do it, a software salesman will do it for Martin, and then I'm not in the room. I'd rather build the machine than be replaced by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out at Calder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Jodie, the part-timer who does the filing three days a week. I'd feel bad about that, I really would. But I don't think it's my job to protect work that a computer does better, it's my job to make the firm run well.

say: I'd say people who **already know the tools** will earn their keep.
I'd volunteer to **run the switchover** at Calder.
think: My job **changes shape** but survives if I lead the change.

Ask for a **new title** and a matching raise.

feel: **Uneasy** but half excited, as long as she's steering.

fieldNote: She plans to **automate her own role** to stay in control of it.

She feels real but limited **guilt** about the part-time filer, Jodie.

steps.text: Automate contractor booking and gas certificate reminders at Calder
Add £100 a month to savings as a buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here and complaining won't change it, so get moving. At church people would be frightened, and I'd try to be practical with them. I'd say families should look after each other, because the government won't be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job at Calder is gone in 2028, no matter how clever I am with the tools. If the AI can do any thinking work, it can run the whole office, including the bit I was going to keep. But Sam's work is hands-on, so he gets about three more years, and that's our lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start running Sam's business side right away, evenings first: quotes, invoices, booking his jobs, a proper website. I'd aim to leave Calder within the year and go full time with Sam, maybe find a second electrician to take on. We'd put the house on hold and keep every bit of the five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have a plan, but I'd be betting both our incomes on one electrician's van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Sam's work when the robots come around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. People might still want a human electrician in their house for a few years after that, because it's their house and their wiring. But I'd be planning for it from day one, not pretending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. A mortgage on a business that might get hit in three years is too big a bet. I'd rather rent a bit longer and have the money ready to move fast.

say: I'd say **complaining won't change** it, so get moving.
I'd tell people at church that **families** must look after each other.
think: My Calder job is **gone in 2028**, however good I am with tools.
Sam's hands-on work gets **three more years**, which is our lifeline.
do: Take over **Sam's business side**: quotes, invoices, bookings and a website.
Leave Calder within the year and **join Sam** full time.
Put the **house on hold** and protect the five months saved.
feel: **Anxious** about betting **both incomes** on one van.
S2.quote: I'd be betting both our incomes on one electrician's van.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots as a household strategy.
She is **honest** that even her tool skills won't save the office job.
Traditional views show in relying on **family, not government**.

steps.text: Run quotes, invoices and bookings for Sam's electrical business evenings
Leave Calder within the year to work for Sam
Put the house purchase on hold and keep renting
Keep the five months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it. At work I'd tell the younger admins to learn a second thing now. I'd post the same in my admin group, and probably get told I'm being dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to build Sam's business into something with two vans and a proper office, and that office would be me. The office work at Calder goes in 2031, but a small electrical firm with good customers keeps earning until around 2034, maybe longer. That's enough time to pay off a van and save a real cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do Sam's books at weekends and build his booking system with AI tools, while staying at Calder for the steady pay. By year two I'd move over and we'd take on an apprentice. We'd put our deposit savings into a second van instead of a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the good kind, where you're too busy to brood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting the house money into a van is a big call. What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say a van before a house is foolish, because he believes in owning your house before anything else. My mum would say Sam's a good man and I know what I'm doing. I'd listen to both and do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you're most aware of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Sam and I fall out over money, honestly. Working with your partner is hard, and he hates being told his paperwork is a mess. We'd have to agree that I run the office and he runs the jobs.

I'd urge younger admins to **learn a second thing** now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who isn't ready by 2036 had fair warning. That sounds hard, I know. But I believe people should take responsibility for their own plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like an opportunity more than a threat. I'd be thirty-seven, with time to buy a house, build Sam's business and maybe start a family. The worry is the end point, because robots come for Sam's work around 2039 and I'd have nothing hands-on to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd stay at Calder and push for the operations role, and do Sam's paperwork on the side. We'd buy the house in the next two years as planned. Around year five I'd move into Sam's firm and start planning for what comes after electricians, maybe managing the robots ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly hopeful. It feels like I can steer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people had fair warning. Would you feel the same about Jodie, the part-timer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, and no, not entirely. Jodie's fifty-two with no interest in computers, so ten years means something different to her. I'd still want her helped, but by her family and her church first, then the government if those run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about work, if you had them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn how things are built and how money works. Those two things never go out of fashion. Everything in between seems to be up for grabs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be pulling my whole income out of Calder and betting it on Sam's van, with only three years before the robots. What would help is cheap small-business loans and plain advice for tradespeople, so firms like Sam's can grow fast. I don't want a handout, I want the red tape cleared.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd trust the AI. I use it every day and I check every single thing it writes. A tool that's right ninety-five times out of a hundred still sends a contractor to the wrong flat once a week.

headlineQuote: A tool that's right ninety-five times out of a hundred still sends a contractor to the wrong flat once a week.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old** admin at a property management firm looking after four hundred rented flats.
She uses AI **every day** and would automate her own job to stay in charge of it.
Her partner Sam's **hands-on electrical work** is her plan B as AGI approaches.
She'd trade the **house deposit** for a second van, against her father's advice.
She believes in **personal responsibility**, family first, but softens for older colleagues like Jodie.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, betting all household income on Sam's business with three years left.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap small-business loans** and plain advice for tradespeople.
